content.text: After the sage Narada had told him the full story of Rama, Valmiki went to bathe in the river Tamasa with his pupil Bharadvaja, marvelling at the clear, pebbled shallow: 'clear as good men's bosoms are.'
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book I Chapter II

content.text: As Valmiki watched, an outcast fowler shot and killed the male of a pair of curlews sporting fearlessly by the bank; the hen bird shrieked in grief over her mate. Moved to sorrow and anger at the cruelty, Valmiki's heart 'with ruth was stirred,' and he pronounced a curse on the fowler in a rhythm he had never spoken before.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book I Chapter II

content.text: Valmiki realized, on reflection, that the words of grief he had cried out had come in perfectly balanced, measured lines — the world's first shloka. He named the new verse-form for the grief (shoka) that had produced it: 'With equal lines of even feet, with rhythm and time and tone complete, the measured form of words I spoke in shock of grief be termed a shloke.'
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book I Chapter II

content.text: That same day, Brahma the Creator himself appeared at Valmiki's hermitage. The sage rose in wondering awe, offered him water and a seat, yet found his mind still returning, unbidden, to the slain curlew — and the verse of grief kept forming on his lips even in the presence of the god.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book I Chapter II

content.text: Brahma smiled and told Valmiki the verse he had spoken unconsciously was itself the sign: 'A verse, unconscious thou hast made; no longer be the task delayed... The tuneful lines thy lips rehearsed spontaneous from thy bosom burst.' He then commissioned Valmiki directly to compose the entire life of Rama in this new verse form, promising: 'In all thy poem, through my grace, no word of falsehood shall have place.'
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book I Chapter II

content.text: Brahma's charge to Valmiki closed with a promise of the epic's endurance: 'As long as in this firm-set land the streams shall flow, the mountains stand, so long throughout the world, be sure, the great Ramayan shall endure... To higher spheres shalt thou arise and dwell with me above the skies!' He then vanished, leaving Valmiki to begin the work.
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book I Chapter II

content.text: Valmiki's own pupils, moved by love of their teacher, took up chanting the verse he had spoken by the river, marvelling at its balanced rhythm — and this became the metre in which Valmiki went on to compose 'hundreds of such verses, sweet with equal lines and even feet,' telling 'the glorious deeds of Rama' in what tradition reveres as the first work of poetry (Adi Kavya), with Valmiki honoured as the first poet (Adi Kavi).
content.source_name: Ralph T. H. Griffith (trans.), The Ramayana of Valmiki (1870-1889), Book I Chapter II
